title: Growth investing (concept)

overview.objective: Own companies whose sales and earnings are growing much faster than average.
overview.context: A concept page. High expected growth is usually already in the price.

simple.simple: [[growth-investing|Growth investing]] means buying companies whose [[revenue]] and [[earnings]] are growing fast, even if the share price looks expensive today.
simple.balanced: A high [[pe-ratio]] means the price already assumes strong growth. If growth merely slows, the share can fall sharply even while the business keeps growing. The [[peg-ratio]] compares price with growth, but only as well as the growth forecast. Issuing new shares ([[dilution]]) spreads earnings more thinly.

reasoning: If a company keeps growing its earnings faster than the market expects, its value could rise more than the high price implies. That is the reasoning; the hard part is that expectations are already high.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true for this fictional company? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional company. Revenue grew from 100 million to 130 million last year. The P/E is 60, and analysts expect earnings to grow 30% a year. It is losing cash and issues about 10% more shares each year.

options.text: Issuing 10% more shares a year dilutes each share's claim on earnings
options.explanation: Right: the same earnings are spread over more shares.

options.text: 30% growth will continue because it did last year
options.explanation: No: past growth is not a promise of future growth.

options.text: A high P/E means the price already assumes strong growth
options.explanation: Right: buyers are paying for growth they expect.

options.text: A P/E of 60 means the price is 60 times revenue per share
options.explanation: No: P/E compares the price with earnings per share, not revenue.

failureAnalysis: Growth slows, and the share falls even though the business still grows.
Forecasts of growth turn out too high.
Cash losses force the company to issue shares, diluting holders.
Rising interest rates can hit highly valued shares hardest.
limitations: This page explains the idea; it gives no rules to pick shares.
Growth forecasts are uncertain, and PEG inherits that uncertainty.
No claim is made that growth investing beats other approaches.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A share has a P/E of 40 and expected earnings growth of 20% a year. What is its PEG ratio?

options.explanation: No: that is 20 ÷ 40, the wrong way round.
Right: P/E divided by the growth rate.

options.text: 800, from multiplying the P/E by the growth rate
options.explanation: No: PEG divides P/E by growth.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What tends to hurt a highly valued growth share most?

options.explanation: Right: the price assumed fast growth.

options.text: A small dividend paid each year
options.explanation: No: a small dividend is common and not a main risk.

options.text: Its number of shares staying exactly the same from one year to the next
options.explanation: No: a steady share count avoids dilution.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Earnings per share are 2.00 and grow 25% a year. What are they after 2 years?

options.explanation: No: that adds 0.50 twice. Growth compounds on the new, larger figure.
No: that is after one year.
